questions_and_answers.question_text: Which English words is it helpful to think of bǐ as?
Where does the bǐ phrase come in the sentence?
What may the two elements being compared be?
Write the Chinese for "Three would be more convenient than two."
Write the Chinese for "He has more free time than I do."
Write the Chinese for "Going by plane is faster than going by train."

answers.answer_text: Zuò fēijī bǐ zuò huǒchē kuài.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "It's more convenient for you to come than for me to go."

answers.answer_text: Nǐ lái bǐ wǒ qù fāngbian.

questions_and_answers.question_text: What part of speech do all elements joined by bǐ act as?
Is bǐ used to say that two things are the same?

answers.answer_text: No — a different pattern is used for that.

articles.text:
5. A: Jīntian xiàwǔ liǎngdiǎn zhōng   Would two o'clock today be convenient?
      fāngbian ma?
   B: Sāndiǎn bǐ liǎngdiǎn fāng-      Three would be more convenient than
      bian yìdiǎnr.                    two.

Note on No. 5

Sāndiǎn bǐ liǎngdiǎn fāngbian yìdiǎnr: Bǐ is a prepositional verb used to make comparisons between two things which are different. In translating, you may find it helpful to think of bǐ as the English "compared with" or "than." Notice that the bǐ phrase precedes the adjectival verb or another predicate in a sentence.

Sāndiǎn | bǐ | liǎngdiǎn | fāngbian yìdiǎn.
(3 o'clock | compared with | 2 o'clock | more convenient)
"Three is more convenient than two."

Tā | bǐ | wǒ | yǒu gōngfu.
(he | compared with | I | have free time)
"He has more free time than I do."

The two elements being compared may be nouns, pronouns, verb phrases, or even full sentences. Actually, all elements joined by bǐ act as nouns, as seen in the English translations of the examples below.

Zuò fēijī | bǐ | zuò huǒchē | kuài.
(ride plane | compared with | ride train | fast)
"Going by plane is faster than going by train."

Nǐ lái | bǐ | wǒ qù | fāngbian.
(you come | compared with | I go | convenient)
"It's more convenient for you to come than for me to go."

(A different pattern is used to say that two things are the same. To say "A is not as... as B," you use a different construction.)
